narrative.text: The table of contents of the cervical pre-cancer screening and treatment guideline, followed by the start of the acknowledgements listing Guideline Development Group members and evidence contributors.
Continues the acknowledgements of the cervical cancer screening guideline, naming observers, WHO Secretariat members and others, and gives the list of acronyms and abbreviations.
A heading for the acronyms and abbreviations section.

Gives the background to the cervical cancer guideline, citing about 604,000 new cases and 342,000 deaths in 2020, mostly in sub-Saharan Africa, Melanesia, South-Eastern Asia and South America. It recalls the Director-General's 2018 call for elimination and the 2020 global strategy targets, and notes that experts agreed to update and simplify screening and treatment recommendations.
A one-line lead-in stating that the updated guideline was developed in three steps.

Lists the three development steps for the cervical cancer guideline: reviewing existing recommendations, framing PICO questions with new or updated systematic reviews and modelling, and applying GRADE with evidence-to-decision tables. It describes the work of the Guideline Development Group from 2019 and defines the screen-and-treat and screen, triage and treat approaches.

Summarises the guideline's 23 recommendations and 7 good practice statements, explaining which apply identically to the general population of women and which differ for women living with HIV. A table pairs the recommendations for each group, starting with the strong recommendation to use HPV DNA detection rather than VIA or cytology as the primary screening test, followed by guidance on triage options, self-collected samples, starting age, screening intervals and follow-up. It gives the strength of each recommendation and certainty of evidence. It ends with summary strategies: HPV DNA screening from age 30 every 5 to 10 years for women generally, and from age 25 every 3 to 5 years with triage for women living with HIV.

Restates the global burden of cervical cancer and the 2030 elimination targets of 90% HPV vaccination, 70% screening and 90% treatment. It explains that cervical intraepithelial neoplasia is caused mainly by high-risk HPV types such as 16 and 18 and distinguishes low-grade lesions from high-grade pre-cancers.

Reviews cervical screening methods, noting that cytology programmes have greatly cut mortality in some countries but have been less successful in low- and middle-income settings, and describes newer VIA and HPV DNA tests and tests under evaluation. A table groups molecular, cytologic and visual inspection tests, and the text explains the screen-and-treat approach, preferably in a single visit.
Defines the two approaches compared in the guideline: screen-and-treat, where treatment follows a positive primary test, and screen, triage and treat, which requires a second positive triage test.

Explains that earlier WHO cervical screening and treatment recommendations were spread across several guidelines and the 2014 comprehensive guide, and that this edition updates them in light of new evidence and the elimination strategy. It states the guideline's objective of improving national screening and treatment strategies for all women, including those living with HIV.

Outlines the four phases of updating WHO's cervical screening recommendations, from updating key algorithms (this guideline) to evaluating others, implementation guidance and a living guideline. It notes that the guideline also aims to clarify starting age, lifetime screens and screening intervals.

Identifies the guideline's audience as policy-makers, programme managers and health professionals involved in cervical cancer prevention, and notes that the term women is used for all people at risk of cervical cancer regardless of gender identity.
A short lead-in stating that the guideline followed the WHO handbook for guideline development and summarising the process.

Describes the groups involved in developing the guideline, including the WHO and IARC Secretariat, Steering Group, Guideline Development Group, External Review Group and systematic review and modelling teams. It notes that much of the work was done virtually through online meetings, surveys and shared platforms.
Explains that Guideline Development Group members completed declarations of interest, which were reviewed and found to raise no conflicts, and were asked to report new interests at each meeting.
Notes that group members signed confidentiality agreements and that discussions and draft recommendations were kept confidential until publication.
Describes the October 2019 scoping review of existing recommendations to decide which to remove, validate, update or add, and the approval of separate then merged scoping documents.

Presents the 14 PICO questions guiding the evidence review, covering comparisons of screen-and-treat and triage strategies, follow-up intervals, starting age and strategies to support screening uptake, some deferred to a later phase.
Explains that a survey and subgroup meeting in December 2019 narrowed the many possible screening and triage combinations to seven priority algorithms for this phase.

Lists the critical outcomes carried over from the 2013 guideline, including cancer incidence and mortality, detection of pre-cancer, preterm birth and grouped adverse events of treatment, along with costs, feasibility and equity.

Describes how evidence was synthesised using WHO and Cochrane methods, drawing on the forthcoming IARC handbook and updating existing reviews where possible. A table maps each type of evidence, such as systematic reviews, modelling and surveys, to the related recommendations.
Summarises the methods used in the systematic reviews, from protocols and database searches to risk-of-bias assessment, synthesis and GRADE certainty ratings.
Describes an individual patient data meta-analysis of age-specific cervical lesion data in women living with HIV, using random-effects models to estimate screening results by age and HIV status.

Explains that the Policy1-Cervix model was used to project outcomes for 78 low- and middle-income countries, with an HIV-HPV model applied to the United Republic of Tanzania. Outcomes modelled included cancer incidence and mortality, treatments, preterm births and cost-effectiveness.
Describes a literature search on values and preferences and an anonymous online survey of 561 women and girls run in English and French in 2020.
Describes a survey of Guideline Development Group members, using the CICI framework, on concerns about implementing each priority algorithm at scale across service components and stakeholder levels.

Explains how evidence-to-decision tables were prepared and discussed virtually, how members gave input and voted through GRADEpro, and how recommendations were finalised. A table explains what strong and conditional recommendations mean for different audiences.

Describes how external peer review comments were handled and how good practice statements were used. It also notes that even one or two lifetime screens can reduce mortality where no routine programme exists and that implementation guidance will follow.

Advises that a multidisciplinary ministry team choose national screening algorithms according to resources, feasibility and acceptability, and distinguishes clinical scenarios for follow-up such as regular screening intervals. It encourages population-based programmes that ensure treatment of women who screen positive.

Stresses screening registries, call-and-recall and links between care levels, and states that screening and treatment should be offered to transgender men, non-binary and intersex people with a cervix, with services made more inclusive.

Describes the screening and triage tests considered, including high-risk HPV DNA tests with partial or extended genotyping, cytology, VIA and colposcopy. It explains how they are combined in algorithms, such as HPV testing followed by VIA triage to decide treatment.

Explains treatment options for cervical pre-cancer, distinguishing ablative methods (thermal ablation, cryotherapy) from excisional ones (LLETZ, cold knife conization), and restates the count of recommendations and good practice statements.

Sets out the recommendations and good practice statements for the general population of women, starting with HPV DNA detection as the preferred primary screening test and covering triage, sample collection, age to start and stop screening, intervals and follow-up. It ends with the summary strategy of HPV DNA screening from age 30 every 5 to 10 years, with or without triage.

Explains the justification for the recommendations, chiefly the greater reductions in cancer and deaths with HPV DNA testing than with VIA or cytology, possible fewer harms and the acceptability of provider or self-sampling. It also justifies the chosen starting age, intervals and follow-up timings, based mostly on low-certainty evidence and modelling.

Summarises the evidence behind the cervical screening recommendations for the general population of women, finding moderate-certainty evidence from trials and modelling that HPV DNA testing reduces pre-cancer, advanced cancer and deaths more than VIA, with lower risk after a negative HPV test than after negative cytology. It reports similar benefits for screen-and-treat and triage approaches, slightly fewer cancers with HPV16/18 genotyping triage, and likely similar performance of self-collected samples. It reviews evidence on starting screening at 30 versus 35, stopping age, screening intervals and follow-up timing, weighing benefits against treatments, preterm births and costs. It notes practical concerns about longer follow-up intervals and the transition from VIA or cytology to HPV testing.

Sets out the recommendations and good practice statements for women living with HIV, including HPV DNA primary screening, use of triage after a positive HPV test, triage options and provider or self-collected samples. It covers starting age, intervals and follow-up after treatment or negative triage, and ends with the summary strategy of HPV DNA screening with triage from age 25 every 3 to 5 years.

Justifies the recommendations for women living with HIV, citing the greater cancer and death reductions from HPV DNA testing, its acceptability and feasibility, and the reduced harms from adding triage. It also explains the chosen screening intervals and follow-up timings, mostly on low-certainty modelled evidence.

Summarises the evidence for the recommendations for women living with HIV, finding that HPV DNA primary screening likely reduces pre-cancer more than VIA and similarly to cytology, and that triage may reduce harms through fewer treatments. It reports modelled benefits of three- to five-year intervals, the likely validity of self-sampling, and a good practice statement to screen at least twice in a lifetime. It also reviews individual patient data and modelling on starting age, follow-up intervals and uncertainties in applying general population results.

Gives a good practice statement to treat women within six months of a decision to treat (deferring until after pregnancy and re-evaluating if delayed) and a conditional recommendation for LLETZ or cold knife conization for adenocarcinoma in situ.

Summarises low-certainty evidence showing little difference in recurrence or complications between cold knife conization and loop excision for adenocarcinoma in situ, but more preterm births after conization, which is also costlier and less accessible. It then lists research gaps on HPV genotyping, screening strategies and starting age for women living with HIV.

Notes further research gaps, including treatment of adenocarcinoma in situ in women living with HIV, cost-effectiveness of excision methods, integrating screening into HIV programmes, loss to follow-up after positive screening, and training costs when moving to HPV testing.

Describes plans to disseminate the cervical screening guideline through WHO networks, its website, printed copies, high-level meetings, conferences and policy briefs, with regional workshops to support national adaptation and partnership with UN agencies.

Continues the dissemination plans, mentioning conferences and supporting WHO guidance, surveys of health workers and clients a year after release to measure impact, and a planned revision of WHO's comprehensive cervical cancer control guide.

Explains that future versions will evaluate further tests such as HPV mRNA, DNA methylation, p16/Ki-67 dual staining and automated visual evaluation, and that Phase 4 will establish living recommendations updated as new evidence emerges.
The reference list for the cervical pre-cancer screening and treatment guideline, citing mainly cancer statistics, WHO strategies and guidance, IARC monographs and screening studies.
Annex 1, listing members of the Guideline Development Group by WHO region and institution, along with other contributors and the WHO and IARC Secretariat.
Annex 2, a table of the evidence-gathering teams and task groups for each set of PICO questions, naming leads and members for reviews, modelling and the IARC handbook.
Annex 3, a table showing that each Guideline Development Group member declared no interests and returned a confidentiality agreement.

Annex 4, listing the seven screening algorithms prioritised for the first phase, two screen-and-treat and five screen, triage and treat, combining VIA, HPV DNA, cytology, genotyping and colposcopy. It presents flow diagrams for each algorithm for the general population and women living with HIV, including follow-up and re-treatment steps.

Annex 5, giving the standardised definitions used in the guideline, starting with eligibility for ablative treatment based on transformation zone type and lesion size and criteria for referral. It defines outcomes such as persistent, residual or recurrent disease and other clinical endpoints used in the reviews. It also defines the treatment methods, including thermal ablation, cryotherapy, LLETZ, cold knife conization and small-loop biopsy. Diagrams illustrate the three types of transformation zone.

Annex 6, giving additional information on quality assurance, screening registries and call-and-recall, and describing the screening tests in more detail, including self-collection of samples, HPV nucleic acid tests and genotyping, cytology and VIA. It advises care in selecting clinically validated HPV tests and ends with footnoted references and WHO contact details.

The cover, ISBN and copyright page of the WHO guideline for screening and treatment of cervical pre-cancer lesions for cervical cancer prevention, second edition (2021), with licence terms and disclaimers.
